title: TorchJD: Stop Averaging Your Losses, Aggregate Their Gradients
hook: Multi-task training usually blends losses into one number before taking a gradient step. TorchJD instead keeps every loss's own gradient and combines them so each one actually goes down.
key_points: Training with multiple losses (multi-task heads, constraints, auxiliary or regularization terms) is usually handled by 'scalarization': combine the losses into one number, then run ordinary gradient descent on it.
TorchJD is an open-source PyTorch library built around an alternative: 'Jacobian descent.'
It computes the Jacobian of the loss vector — one gradient per individual loss, not one blended gradient — before taking a step.
Those per-loss gradients are then aggregated into a single update vector chosen to decrease each loss, rather than trading one off against another implicitly.
Positioned as a drop-in alternative for PyTorch training loops that already juggle multiple objectives.
content_html: Most PyTorch training loops that juggle several losses — a multi-task model, an auxiliary objective, a regularization term — handle it the same way: add them up (maybe with some weights) into one scalar, then call backward on that. TorchJD, an open-source library shared by its author on r/MachineLearning, argues this "scalarization" throws away information you could be using.
extra_html: The alternative TorchJD implements is "Jacobian descent": instead of collapsing the loss vector into one number before differentiating, it computes the Jacobian — a separate gradient for each individual loss — and only then aggregates those gradients into a single parameter update. The aggregation is chosen so the update tends to decrease each loss, rather than implicitly trading one off against another the way a weighted sum can. It's presented as a practical drop-in for PyTorch code already training on multiple losses, tasks, or constraints.

related.title: Adam: The Default Optimizer
related.hook: Adam gives every parameter its own adaptive step size by tracking the gradient's recent average and spread — and it mostly just works.

related.title: AdamW: Decoupled Weight Decay
related.hook: L2 regularization and weight decay are the same thing for plain SGD - but not for Adam. Decoupling them fixes Adam's generalization and makes the best decay value independent of the learning rate.

flashcards.prompt: What is 'scalarization' in multi-loss training, and what does TorchJD do instead?
flashcards.back_html: Scalarization combines multiple losses into a single number (e.g. a weighted average) before running gradient descent. TorchJD instead keeps each loss's own gradient separate and aggregates them into one update.

flashcards.prompt: What does 'Jacobian descent' compute that plain scalarization skips?

choices.text: The Jacobian of the loss vector — one gradient per individual loss — before aggregating into an update
A second-order Hessian for every parameter
A single averaged loss value with no per-loss gradient info

flashcards.explanation_html: Scalarization blends losses first, losing per-loss gradient information. Jacobian descent keeps one gradient per loss (the Jacobian) and aggregates them afterward, aiming to decrease each loss rather than an averaged proxy.

flashcards.prompt: In what training scenarios would a library like TorchJD be relevant?
flashcards.back_html: Any setup with multiple objectives trained jointly — multi-task heads, hard constraints, auxiliary losses, or regularization terms — where combining them into one scalar loss can obscure how each one is actually behaving.
